This looks interesting. “How to Improve Your Presentation Skills.” Most people rarely enjoy giving presentations, do they? I get so nervous. Maybe this can give me something to help me focus when I am giving one. Let's see ...

“Number one, a good presentation is planned with the end in mind. Decide exactly how you want your presentation to be received. Is it your intention to persuade your audience? Do you want to inspire them?  Do you want to inform them? The purpose of your presentation needs to be made clear from the start.

“Next, keep it simple.” Of course. People are more engaged by presentations that are easy to follow. You rarely pay attention to a dense and complex presentation, do you? “Don't wing it, but don't memorize it. A presentation needs to be practiced out loud and delivered naturally.”
This is interesting ... “Speak in questions. There are two types of presenters. There are those presenters who see themselves as experts in a particular area. There are others who prefer to facilitate. They get people to converse. They want their audience to ask questions and explore possibilities, so they make their environment conducive to doing just that. To make this happen, they include questions in their presentation.” You hardly ever hear questions, do you? That's something to think about.

contents.value:
Sophie: Kelly, what's the best way to prepare a presentation?
Kelly: Well, first you need to think about the purpose. Do you want to inform, persuade, or inspire? Don't start writing until you know your purpose.
Sophie: Okay. Then what?
Kelly: Remember to keep it simple. Don't try to include too much information. It should be easy to follow.
Sophie: Should I use Powerpoint?
Kelly: You can, but only have 3 bullets per slide. And always include some questions in your presentation. They engage your listeners and encourage exploring possibilities.

You use tag questions in spoken English to get clarification and confirmation.
Sometimes they are used in an affirmative sentence but with a negative adverb.
Question tags are short questions at the end of statements.
They are mainly used in speech when we want to:

• confirm that something is true or not, or
  • to encourage a reply from the person we are speaking to.

A positive statement is followed by a negative question tag.
Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying ‘yes'.

Some adverbs always infer the negative. These are adverbs such as: rarely, never, seldom, scarcely and hardly. They change the feeling of a sentence from positive to negative. Therefore, statements including these adverbs become negative statements. This means that when a question tag is added, it will be a positive one.

To deliver a great presentation there are some skills that you need. The skills below will help you make your presentation a great one.

• Start by considering the end.
    • Decide what you want your presentation to do. Do you want it to persuade, inform or inspire?
    • Develop a presentation that includes all the necessary components.

• Keep it simple.
    • Don't try to put too much information in the presentation.
    • Keep PowerPoint slides simple. (3 bullet points per slide)

• Don't wing it, but don't memorize.
    • Only the important sections of your speech need to be memorized.
    • Use cue cards if you need to make notes.
    • Practice your presentation out loud.

• Include lots of questions.
    • Use questions in your presentation to engage and persuade others.

• Focus on quality, not quantity.
    • Choose a specific idea to anchor your talk and build your presentation around it.

• Smile!
    • During the presentation, smile, take deep breaths, and pause.
